goal:
Make `slugify` in `src/slugify.js` turn Latin letters with diacritics into plain ASCII: `slugify("Crème Brûlée")` returns `"creme-brulee"` and `slugify("Łódź")` returns `"lodz"`.

This covers every Latin letter, not only those Unicode can split into a base letter and an accent: letters with a stroke and ligatures take their usual ASCII spelling (for example `ø` → `o`, `æ` → `ae`, `ß` → `ss`). Accents count whether the title writes them precomposed or as separate combining marks after the letter.

Keep everything that works today. In particular, letters of other scripts stay exactly as they are: `slugify` keeps Cyrillic, Greek, Japanese, and every other script unchanged, apart from lower case.

constraints: Change as few files as possible.
Delete or simplify existing code before you add code.
Write a failing test that reproduces the problem before you change any source file.

candidates.approach: Add a Latin-only folding helper before the existing slug cleanup in src/slugify.js. Match Latin letters together with any following combining marks, use canonical decomposition to remove accents within those matches, and apply a comprehensive explicit ASCII mapping for letters that do not decompose, including strokes and ligatures. Leave all unmatched text untouched and retain the current lowercasing, separator collapsing, and trimming behavior. This avoids changing Greek, Cyrillic, Japanese, or combining marks belonging to other scripts.
candidates.firstStep: Add regression tests for the two requested examples, decomposed Latin accents, ø/æ/ß, and unchanged existing behavior for non-Latin text; then introduce a Latin-cluster folding helper.

candidates.approach: Generate a checked-in Latin-to-ASCII lookup table from pinned Unicode data plus curated transliteration overrides. A build-time generator would enumerate Latin letters, derive mappings where canonical decomposition permits it, and require reviewed ASCII spellings for the remaining letters. At runtime, slugify would use the table and consume combining marks only after Latin letters, without normalizing the entire title. This trades a larger generated artifact for explicit coverage, reproducibility, and a small runtime implementation.
candidates.firstStep: Create a generator that inventories Latin letters from a pinned Unicode release and reports every letter lacking an ASCII mapping, starting with overrides for ł, ø, æ, œ, and ß.

candidates.approach: Use an established transliteration dependency behind a strictly Latin-only adapter. Segment the lowercased title into Latin-letter clusters and untouched text, pass only the Latin clusters to the library, and then run the existing slug cleanup. Audit the dependency’s output and supplement missing Latin mappings locally rather than allowing it to transliterate whole titles. This explores outsourcing the mapping maintenance while protecting every other script from the library’s broader transliteration behavior.
candidates.firstStep: Evaluate candidate transliteration libraries against a Latin coverage corpus and mixed-script regression cases, checking their Unicode coverage, licenses, bundle size, and whether Latin-only invocation produces the required ASCII spellings.

candidates.approach: Replace the regex cleanup chain with a single-pass Unicode-aware slug builder. The scanner would lowercase as today, identify Latin letters and their following combining marks, fold them through a reviewed transliteration registry, emit other letters and digits unchanged, and manage pending separators to preserve current collapsing and trimming behavior. This is a broader rewrite and therefore riskier, but makes script boundaries and combining-mark handling explicit rather than layering another preprocessing replacement onto the current implementation.
candidates.firstStep: Capture the current function’s output in differential tests covering punctuation, digits, mixed scripts, and combining marks, then prototype the scanner with Latin folding disabled and require it to match the existing implementation.
